It is unfortunate that this game is flooded with so many negative reviews because they are scaring people off of coming to one of the most fun shooters I've played since Titanfall 2. So at the end of the day I'd like to say this one simple thing. 

Just try it.

# Mecha BREAK: A Competitive Game That Somehow Forgot to Build a Competitive Scene

Mecha BREAK is a spectacular-looking game wrapped around one of the most poorly thought-out competitive ecosystems I have seen in a PvP game. The actual mech combat can be fun, but almost everything surrounding it feels like the developers had absolutely no idea what kind of competitive game they were trying to build.

Amazing Seasun had plenty of experience with online games, but they had never established themselves as developers of a serious arena-based PvP game. Yet Mecha BREAK came out swinging with ranked systems, competitive aspirations, and even the apparent ambition of building an esports scene almost immediately. And it failed hard.

Instead of spending years building a healthy competitive ecosystem, establishing matchmaking, understanding player behavior, refining ranked progression, and then seeing whether an esports scene naturally develops, the game seemed determined to shove competitive gaming down everyone's throat from day one. The result is a competitive scene that is difficult to take seriously.

## Ranked Matches With Bots

Having bots in a PvP game is already questionable. Having bots in ranked matches is absurd. Having bots in ranked matches while simultaneously trying to present the game as a serious competitive title is next-level stupidity.

Then there is the complete lack of meaningful rank decay at the top. Watching a supposedly competitive leaderboard where players can sit in the Top 100 without meaningful rank decay is one of the dumbest competitive systems I have ever seen. A leaderboard is supposed to represent who is actively competing and performing well, instead Mecha BREAK can turn it into a museum exhibit. And somehow this gets even worse.

## The Blocklist Problem

The fact that players can influence matchmaking through their blocklists is genuinely baffling. If your matchmaking system allows competitive players to manipulate who they are matched against by strategically blocking people, then your competitive integrity is already hanging by a thread.

This becomes catastrophic in smaller regions. EU is the perfect example. When the active high-level population becomes small enough that the same players repeatedly encounter each other, top players can share blocklists and effectively manipulate the matchmaking pool. At that point, what exactly are we measuring? Mechanical skill? Team coordination? Who can manipulate the matchmaking system most effectively? Who has the right people blocked? Who can avoid the players they don't want to fight?

Congratulations, you have accidentally turned ranked matchmaking into social engineering. This makes statements from Kris, who apparently believes he knows what gamers want better than the gamers themselves, increasingly difficult to take seriously. If this is the direction the competitive design is heading, perhaps making mobile games would have been the more appropriate career path, because whatever Mecha BREAK is trying to accomplish competitively clearly isn't working.

## The "Competitive Scene" Is a Joke

The smaller the region, the worse this becomes. When you have fewer than 100 genuinely active players in a competitive region and those players can influence matchmaking through blocklists, the entire ranking system becomes questionable. You cannot build a legitimate competitive environment out of a population that small while simultaneously allowing players to manipulate the matchmaking pool.

Yet apparently this is supposed to become an esports game. An esports game needs a stable player population, strong matchmaking, transparent competitive rules, meaningful ranking systems, serious anti-abuse mechanisms, and a healthy ecosystem. Mecha BREAK has managed to make several of those things optional. But don't worry, at least we have another overpriced cosmetic bundle.

## Progression and Currency Systems

The progression system is another mess. There are too many currencies, too many systems, and too many layers between the player and the actual content they want. Instead of making progression feel rewarding, it often feels like the game is constantly trying to figure out which currency it can put between you and the thing you actually want.

The player should be thinking: **"What do I want to unlock?"** Instead, Mecha BREAK frequently makes you think: **"Which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ currency do I need for this?"** That is not satisfying progression. That is an accounting department disguised as a game.

## Communication From the Developers

The communication doesn't exactly inspire confidence either. Competitive games require developers who understand that their community needs clear explanations, especially when it comes to matchmaking, ranking, progression, seasonal systems, and competitive integrity.

Instead, players are frequently left trying to figure out what the developers actually intend. When developers appear convinced that they understand what players want better than the players themselves, the disconnect becomes even more obvious. A developer can disagree with its community, that's fine, but if the community repeatedly tells you that something is broken and your response is essentially "you don't know what you want," eventually you have to consider the possibility that the problem isn't the customers.

## Too Many Modes, Not Enough Players

This might be the most obvious mathematical problem in the entire game. You have multiple game modes, ranked, different team sizes, extraction, different regions, and then a shrinking player population. What could possibly go wrong? Everything.

Instead of concentrating the remaining players into a healthy matchmaking pool, Mecha BREAK spreads them across multiple queues and then apparently has to use bots to fill the holes. This creates a death spiral: **fewer players → longer queues → bots → worse matches → players leave → fewer players.** And then the solution apparently is another game mode. Fantastic.

## The Biggest Problem

The biggest problem with Mecha BREAK isn't that the game is terrible. That's actually what makes it frustrating. There is a genuinely fun mech game buried underneath all of this. The combat can be fantastic, the mechs look incredible, and the core concept is strong.

And yet the developers seem determined to surround that good foundation with questionable competitive design, bloated progression, excessive monetization, fragmented matchmaking, and a baffling approach to player feedback. The studio had never established itself as a serious arena PvP developer and nevertheless seemed eager to push Mecha BREAK toward esports immediately.

Instead of building the foundation first, they tried to build the trophy room. Now the foundation is cracking: bots in ranked, no meaningful top-rank decay, matchmaking that can be influenced through blocklists, tiny regional populations, players manipulating who they encounter, multiple queues splitting the remaining population, progression systems designed like a spreadsheet, overpriced cosmetics, oversexualized character monetization, repetitive content, poor communication, and balance problems.

Mecha BREAK didn't need to become an esports game on day one. It needed to become a good competitive game first. Instead, the developers tried to sell us the esports fantasy before proving they could build the ecosystem. The result is a competitive scene that increasingly feels less like professional PvP and more like a private lobby with a leaderboard attached.

The sad part is that the mech combat deserved better.

Another mech game where you dream of what could have been. Poor decisions by the developers have hamstrung this one out of the gate, with aggressive microtransactions, poor perception handling on 'pay to win' (it's not, but communication is the larger issue) mechanics, and progression that is not competitive with other free-to-play games in this category.

Now that the game has hemorrhaged players, most games are filled with bots up until you hit Grandmaster Tier (not impressive, it does not take very long to get there). Bots are a double-edged sword, and easily one of the biggest threats to the game's longevity. They are necessary to even play nowadays, given the shrunken playerbase. What is a problem is how they are handled - specifically, the experience of slogging through a team full of bots - your own teammate bot AI significantly worse. 

All bots have exceptional auto-aim, are able to pivot onto your mech from one attack to pinpoint where you are, and have frame-perfect movement and the ability to see through stealth. Again - if you have a group of six players vs. bots, you will be fine. If you are 1-2 players and 4-5 bots, this is like pulling teeth with a visually flashy pair of pliers. The experience of grinding through your matches with your own bots staring at walls or sluggishly moving back and forth while the enemy bot team works in perfect coordination is discouraging at best and rage-inducing at worst. What remains of PVP balance errs on the side of caution rather than reactivity - however, the devs are not striking this balance correctly, with some strikers remaining an issue across seasons. 

They are planning to re-release this game in July as an 'updated' version addressing some of the issues. This was announced in November 2025. What they have not done since then is provide a roadmap as to what changes they will have. I personally do not have high hopes.

I'll start by saying a lot of these reviews are wrong about some fundamental things (like PvE content). I explain a little furthur in.

Anyway, I waited for the devs to announce their plans for season 4 before trying this game. From the outside looking in, with dozens upon dozens of amazing games vying for my attention, I just don't have the time to invest into a game that isn't going to be around in another 3 months. I also found the strong PvP focus a turn-off. 

Thankfully, the Season 4 changes look promising (assuming they follow through with a greatly reduced team). Also, the game is damn good fun, pretty, and responsive. 

I want to clear up some misinformation I'm seeing in the other reviews: 

1) There IS solo PvE content (and not just the prologue). You can join Mishmak in covert ops (no enemy teams) and launch without matchmaking. It isn't the same as a full-fledged story mode (or horde mode, roguelite mode, etc), but it allows you to progress and practice using some of the mechs in various scenarios. Additionally, you can try any Striker in training mode whether you own them or not. 

2) The monetization is not aggressive. It just isn't. There are things that are outrageously expensive, but they're also cosmetic (and, if I'm brutally honest, most are hideous beyond all reason). For the, "I wish I could pay once and get everything" crowd. You can drop 10 bucks on the season pass, get a premium Striker right away and, within a few hours, get another one. I'm well on my way to a third and I literally just started. That gives me seven Strikers to play (and I made informed decisions on who to pick thanks to training mode) and each will take dozens of hours to truly master.

There are some things I find frustrating, but that's true of any high-skillcap game I've ever played. The biggest is the number of bots in online PvP matches. However, without them, lower ranks would be completely barren.

TLDR: This game isn't for everyone, but there are a ton of players who would love it who are missing out due to an insane amount of misinformation. It's mostly a PvP game, but there is plenty of PvE to do as well (once you find it) and the monetization is not nearly as bad as everyone makes it out to be. I recommend if you're even remotely interested.

I picked up this game a year after release. As far as I can tell, most people consider it a dead game. Well, it may be on life support, but it's not dead and I hope it doesn't die. The truth is that this is a pretty fantastic game. If you're looking for a game that merges a Gundam-esque theme with Overwatch style gameplay, you've found it.

I'll break down my experiences into some pros and cons for you to consider if it's right for you:


[h1]Pros[/h1]

[h3]The visuals are phenomenal[/h3]
They nail the aesthetic of Gundam-like mechs. The particle effects are well done, and the environments are generally well constructed to place you in the themes of the shows and games many have enjoyed before.

[h3]The gameplay is sharp[/h3]
Abilities feel crisp and movement feels reliable. Certain mechs aren't just fast, but feel fast. Abilities that provide indicators before delivery do a good job of cutting through the chaos to give everyone time to react, allowing for counterplays. Timing of abilities feel like they keep the pace of the battle flowing well. I also like that there aren't a million different crowd control effects that last too long. What exists is disruptive without being overbearing.

[h3]The customization is deep[/h3]
I love that I can customize my mech's colors across so many areas, making it feel unique and fresh. It gives me something to do when I'm waiting in queue. The pilot is pretty goonin', but the same is still true. This is something I've come to appreciate over time.

[h1]Cons[/h1]

[h3]The menus are messy[/h3]
There's just too many menus and places to click. You also go down chains that you'd expect to link back on their own, but don't. It's a minor thing, but one you notice and feel frustration with. It's the result of a game that seemed like they had developers come up with good ideas and slammed them into the game without cohesion, resulting in menu hell in some cases. For the most part, this is a minor gripe, but enough time spent and it wears you down.

[h3]Bots in matchmaking[/h3]
This sounds like it was a contributing cause of the game's decline, but became a necessary evil with just 1,300 active people. However, the game does everything it can to mask whether or not you're partied with or against bots. It does this to hide the fact that the game is kinda empty. The frustration with this is that sometimes the bots are really good and other times they're absolutely braindead. Some modes like Ace Arena seem to amplify this. If they're going to keep the bots in matches, then they need to improve the consistency of the AI. Do the challenge missions as a new player and you'll discover that the bots can be challenging! 

[h3]Ranks need to be reduced[/h3]
There's just too many of them with no point. It isn't until you reach grand master that you can only be paired with humans, which actually becomes detrimental due to the volume of people playing (so sad). You go through a somewhat lengthy climb just to arrive at a point where ranked leads to super long queues. You end up just running casual mode most of the time. 

[h3]Currencies are confusing[/h3]
Because the game also has in-game purchases and pve modes, there are other currencies that I don't even understand. The game doesn't do a good job of explaining things here or helping to get me involved in the pve side of the game. It feels pretty half baked, and the marketplace where you list off stuff feels extremely incomplete. It's like they have the elements for a foundation, but nothing actually put together for a well-rounded player experience.


[h1]Fries in the basket[/h1]
This game is just fun. It's been an absolute blast getting some buddies together and experiencing it as a group. We've had such a great time and we'd love to see more people join in. We live in a time where we expect games to be better than this, but it's often the window dressing that we make a big deal about. The core aspects of the game are great, and worth seeing succeed. I'm kinda shilling the game a bit because the potential for greatness is all right there. IF they pump the right modes and cut the fat, relaunch to bring in fresh blood, I think we'd have the mech game many of us wanted and didn't know it.

Give it an honest try, but grab 1-2 friends.

The more I play, the less fun it becomes — especially since most players only care about kill counts and completely ignore objectives.

The developers have the ability to rebalance the game every patch or update, but they choose not to. Instead, they release overpriced skins. It’s already been four seasons, and nothing has changed. Honestly, skins should cost around 50–250 Corite at most.

On top of that, there’s no Raid mode or meaningful story content. The gameplay design shouldn’t be overly punishing, and the game should include proper difficulty options like Easy, Normal, and Hard modes.

Until the developers acknowledge and address these problems, I can’t recommend this game. They should take notes from Final Fantasy XIV, where tanks and healers can sustain themselves and provide strong crowd control effectively.

I’ll wait and see if improvements are made. If the game gets properly updated and balanced, I might change my mind.

You still find bots, and not just a few, like a lot, and they will absolutely ruin your game.  You also find players who aren't competitive, because of paid "rank loss prevention."  This means that if you're playing poorly, you can stay at the same rank, and continue climbing instead of having to be stuck with your poor gameplay. It ruins any sort of meaning to ranked structure, and I've played many games competitive games (AOE2, StarCraft series, Halo series, League of Legends, Overwatch, CoD, BF, and more...). 4.  Voice acting:  honestly this is a nit pick as far as Im concerned, but holy hell is this incredibly repetitive.  If you're into anime (I am not), then this won't be a bother to you but jeeezus is there soooo much anime high pitched, over-the-top voice acting.  ughh.  If it weren't mutable, I wouldn't play it.

If you grew up watching Armored Core, Gundam, or Zone of the Enders and wanted a game that captures that blistering, high-speed tactical robot warfare in a modern multiplayer format, Mecha BREAK is an absolute masterpiece in the making. It delivers pure, unadulterated adrenaline.

The Good:
[list]
[*]Breathtaking Speed and Combat: The movement mechanics feel incredible. The transition between high-speed aerial dodging, ground dashing, and shifting into jet forms is seamless. Every melee clash feels heavy and impactful, while long-range artillery strikes feel devastating.

[*]Diverse Mecha Lineup: The game doesn't just offer skin swaps; every single mech (Striker) has a completely distinct archetype and mechanical identity. Whether you want to play a massive, shield-bearing heavy tank, a stealthy sniper, a flying support healer, or a lightning-fast melee assassin, there is a mech tailored to your exact playstyle.

[*]Insane Customization: The paint and cosmetic customization suite is incredibly detailed. You can modify specific armor plates, weathering effects, glows, and matte/metallic finishes to build your dream custom rig.

[*]Tactical Team Play: The 3v3 and 6v6 modes require genuine coordination. It’s not just a mindless deathmatch; combining a heavy defender's shield with a sniper's covering fire to protect an objective feels highly rewarding.
[/list]
The Mixed:
[list]
[*]The visual chaos can be overwhelming at first. With missiles, lasers, and thruster plumes filling the screen, it takes a few matches to develop the spatial awareness needed to track fast-moving targets.
[/list]
It is easily one of the most fluid, visually spectacular, and mechanically satisfying mech games on the market right now. If you want high-octane metal-on-metal violence, this is a mandatory download.

As a devout 'single player games will always be better than online multiplayer ones' kind of guy, I gotta say, Mecha Break is pretty fun.

In terms of moment-to-moment gameplay, Mecha Break is really fun. Fast combat, snappy controls, and there's actually quite a bit of variety in the mechs, to the point that I can't say any of the current lineup is any similar to any other ones. You've got the drill-spear mech, the stealth sniper mech, the [i]air[/i] sniper mech, the absolute tank mech, plane mech, heal mech, the list goes on. I want to say that some could use a bit of tuning (looking at you Welkin), but it's possible that I just suck at certain matchups. The mechs and moment-to-moment gameplay carries the whole game, I think. Because outside of that, I wouldn't say Mecha Break sets any standards.

For the content, I admit I'm not sure I can be a proper judge for it, because I usually hate multiplayer online PvP games and am not very familiar with them, but by itself, Mecha Break feels a tad lacking. You've got the default 6v6 mode with several different types of missions, you've got the 3v3 arena that's basically just a Deathmatch mission from the 6v6 mode, and you've got the extraction shooter mode that seems to have hardly any players and also seems to be the only feasible way to earn any amount of the premium currency as an F2P, because you can sell your loot in the in-game marketplace and pray to the mech gods that someone will buy.

That's also my main criticism, I suppose: there's hardly any way for F2P to earn premium currency; not even a pittance. Most cosmetics, notably outfits, can only be bought with premium currency too, so as someone who loves cosmetic options in games, I can only ask the mech gods why.

Back to the game modes, specifically the ranked 6v6 one. It is ranked, and you get rewards at the end of every season. The rewards? Lootboxes. Yeah, grind your weekend away, place well, and you get a [i]chance[/i] of rolling...something. Is this the standard for online PvP games? I wouldn't know, but if it is, good lord. I'm not even sure what significant thing you can get out of the lootboxes. Most I've gotten out of them are paltry amounts of seasonal points and dupes upon dupes of paintjobs for the mechs that I'll never use because I already have a favourite--and also most of them look like old carpet.

The seasonal points are used as currency, by the way; you use them to buy newly-released mechs (not the default lineup; those are free), items for the extraction mode, and that's about it. There are cosmetics that you can buy with them, but they're locked behind the premium pass. Yeah, you need to spend money to get the privilege to spend in-game money.

And that's about it, I suppose. Good gameplay, everything else is ehhhhhhhhhhhhhhh. I've been picking it up from time to time since launch, and while I enjoy my short bursts of mech on mech action, there isn't really much incentive to keep playing. Still, I recommend at least to check it out, if not only for the mechs and gameplay.

Honestly the most fun team hero/class shooter I've ever played in the gameplay department.  There is strong mecha influence in the lock-on system (FCS), fluid armor, and energy bar (EN) mechanics.  There is a lot of interesting mobility as well, as literally every mech in the game can boost and hover around.  The game is free-to-play, so be ready to see a lot of cosmetics microtransaction options like in other hero shooters, but it is not pay-to-win.  Word of warning: the game is somewhat harsh and pretty difficult to master.  There are no ultimate abilities, healing is a lot lighter than in other hero shooters, and the aforementioned FCS, fluid armor, and EN mechanics are extremely unforgiving when they are disrupted.  Looking forward to the PlayStation release adding a bunch of new players.

Note: There are 3 modes of gameplay, Operation VERGE (6v6 PvP with objectives), Operation STORM a.k.a 'Mashmak' (Extraction Shooter-esque PvPvE), and Ace Arena (3v3 PvP deathmatch).  Pretty much 90% of my time playing is in VERGE, so that's most of what this review is for.  A lot of people have fun with the Mashmak, but it's not really my cup of tea. Mecha break will obviously pull comparisons to Armored core 6, but the main difference between Mecha break and Armored core is a big one:

Mecha break is faster paced, and doesn't rely on you grinding for days or longer to unlock "the good parts" that you can actually use to play online, nor does it suffer from AC6's biggest flaw, the stamina system. No, not the ENERGY system. The stamina-break system. The stamina break system limited AC6 in SO many ways, and while it's absolutely possible to have a few fun rounds with friends using meme parts, if you go into any form of quickplay, you'll run into legions of the same minmaxed AC's.

Mecha break snaps that in half by making each mech it's own unique hero, more akin to something like overwatch or titanfall, where it plays more like a hero shooter, with each Mecha (called strikers) having a unique, interesting kit that stands them apart from the rest. But what this does is encourage players to pick something that suits their sensibilities and playstyle, but offers a few variants on that style, usually by weight class.

The game features a PLETHORA of modes, and by this time tomorrow as of the time of posting this review, we'll also have a co-op roguelike mode.

So you have:

•  6v6, Ranked and Unranked.
•  3v3, Ranked and Unranked.
• 1~3 player PVE co-op Roguelike modes.
• 1~3 player extraction-shooter style modes, as well as a 1~3 Co-op PVE variant where the AI is more dangerous.
• A 12 player free-for-all mode.

Oh and from time to time they also run events that include things like co-op boss raids.

So you have A PLETHORA of modes that allow you to pick what you're in the mood for, PVP or PVE, and you could absolutely play the game entirely in one mode or the other if that's all you want, or mix-and-match across the gamut to maximize your rewards and boost your credits up faster.

If you're even REMOTELY competent, you can scrounge up the credits you need to unlock one of the handful of locked strikers in a few hours. You do have the option to skip the "wait" but it's barely a wait, honestly. There's paid games out there that make you grind more for unlocks and not by a little. This game is GENEROUS, with a striker unlock having a cost of 15'000, and each individual game you play averaging around 300~600 depending on your performance, and if double-credit weekend bonuses are going, and each mission gives you an extra 1000 which you can do 6 of a week. So if you do your weeklies, by the time you finish those, you'll EASILY have enough for a new Striker every single week and that's assuming you're taking your time.

In the time I've been playing, I've already got 4 of them.

OH AND THEY GIVE YOU A FREE TRIAL OF ONE OF THE LOCKED STRIKERS EVERY WEEK FOR YOU TO PLAY AND EVEN IF YOU OWN THEM ALREADY, YOU CAN DO BONUS MISSIONS WITH THEM FOR EVEN **MORE** free credits.

You can easily, if you play consistently and diligently, milking every single credit out of the game you can, get every single locked striker for free in a month. That's nothing to sneeze at when it comes to free to play games. That's damn near UNHEARD OF in my 30 years of playing MMO's and F2P games.

And with movement smoother than silk, Combat that naturally flows, and the unique customization systems such as having skins drop from just playing the game for free (In large numbers, mind you) and each one being unique even in it's own type? IE: If you have "Jungle stripe" and I have "Jungle stripe", our two camos might be completely different colors, in different positions, with different logos, but share the same "design" overall. So, first things first, I am biased because, as I suspect [i]most[/i] of the playerbase is, a massive Mecha fan, much like the developers themselves.

Gameplay is good, fluid, and fast. Each of the individual Strikers feel unique, even if they have overlaps in their niches - Skyraider is more suited to direct combat while Falcon is more suited to hit-and-runs, Aquila's sniping is meant to be done at a much closer range as compared to Narukami's, Stego and Inferno are both Ultra-Heavy Attackers but have entirely different playstyles, etc...

It's also a passion project - with all the pros and cons that implies. On the one hand, it means that this game is liable to get a lot of updates and regular support; on the other hand, balance patches and big game-changers may be long in coming.

Now, there are [i]very[/i] few games that manage to correctly convey the feeling of controlling a Mecha (that is to say, those giant robots that lie on the more humanoid side of the scale) - and unfortunately most Mecha games make it rather difficult to distinguish between a mecha and a powered armor. And I can confidently say that Mecha BREAK is not one of them, On the gameplay side, while movement feels fluid, it also feels [i]weighty[/i] and satisfying. High TTK even for the [i]light[/i] Strikers helps sell the fact that these things are technically heavy weapons by infantry metrics. Every Striker usually has some form of mounted weapon and/or ability entirely separate from their handheld weapons, often multiple.

On the aesthetic side, you're always reminded that these things are, in fact, [i]weapons platforms[/i] - many have elements that would be impossible or inconvenient on a suit, the Strikers in general resemble [i]robots[/i] more than they do [i]armor[/i] (likely courtesy of having veteran mechanical designers on-board), scattered around every map are human-scale objects that your Striker dwarfs, actual sustained flight is something only a select few Strikers are actually capable of, etc - It all helps convey that sense of "this is a giant robot" that, to my knowledge, only Armored Core has mananged to nail before.

Mecha BREAK is fairly easy to get started with, but difficult to get really good at.

While mechs within the same class have some overlap, each one still has its own mechanics that you need to learn. There is a bit of a rock-paper-scissors feel between different mechs, but skill matters a lot. If you're better with your mech than the other player is with theirs, you can absolutely win even when the matchup isn't in your favor.

The game looks simple at first, but there's a surprisingly high skill ceiling. New players will probably need some time to figure things out. The unfortunate part is that matchmaking doesn't seem to care much about account age or experience. It's not uncommon to end up against players who have been playing much longer than you, which can be frustrating when you're still trying to learn the basics.

There's also a PvE mode, and it's honestly a good way to build up currency and unlock mechs that fit your playstyle better. The catch is that you need an item earned through PvP to enter, so new players can't completely avoid PvP if they want to progress that way.

I originally played this on PC but didn't stick with it for long. I only really got back into the game after getting a Steam Deck. Surprisingly, it runs pretty well. Cap it at 45 FPS and the experience is smooth enough for a competitive game.

What I ended up liking most is how well it fits handheld gaming. Most matches last around 10–15 minutes, so it's easy to squeeze in a game during a break, while waiting for something, or whenever you have a bit of free time.

Overall, if you enjoy mecha games and don't mind learning mechanics, Mecha BREAK is worth trying. The gameplay is fun, each mech feels distinct, and I'd definitely recommend giving it a shot on Steam Deck.

That said, I really think the game needs better ways for new players to learn and play against others at a similar experience level. The biggest obstacle right now isn't the gameplay, it's surviving long enough to learn it.

I was pretty excited for this game when it was first announced. A shiny new fast-paced mecha action game for me to sink my teeth into. The graphics looked great, and most importantly, the mech designs were awesome (Falcon, my beloved). But upon hearing about the disastrous launch, I decided to refrain from downloading the game. It sounded to me like just another poorly thought-out live-service cash grab (and my hunch was proven correct).

Fast forward to the recent dev update. Hearing about how the team had been filtered down to only developers who truly care about this game and want it to succeed gave me a bit of hope. They sounded so genuine, filled with passion to improve, to course-correct, and to bring out the game’s true potential. The addition of the PvE roguelike mode sealed the deal. I would finally try out Mecha Break.

After finishing character creation, I was wowed by the tutorial mission. What a bombastic way to start a mech game. Sure, it was a bit janky. The animations were stiff at times, and the cutscenes were locked at 30 FPS for some reason. But the heart was there. I was once again reminded of how much wasted potential there was in releasing this game as a PvP experience instead of a single-player one. They could have told far more interesting stories in the world they created. Hell, it might have even spawned a whole new IP.

Nevertheless, this is the game we got, and I continued on to try out the PvP mode. It’s pretty decent. Fast-paced, the mechs all do different things, and there’s room for strategy and skill expression. Nothing amazing, but nothing horrible either. My one question is: if this was supposed to be a highly competitive esport game, then why does account/PvE progression give players an advantage in PvP matches? This was one of the biggest questions I had at launch, and one of the main reasons I was put off by the game. But PvP aside, now it was time for the most important part of the update: the roguelike mode. 

[b]It’s a training simulation…[/b]

Imagine my disappointment when I found out that the roguelike mode is merely a virtual training simulation. A horrible decision both gameplay-wise and immersion-wise. For one, it completely isolates the mode from the rest of the game’s story landscape, relegating it to little more than a side activity. Second, it drops you into a bland training map where you shoot at basic enemies standing around on flat ground. It also seems that the devs have, for some incomprehensible reason, decided to balance the mode around mod progression, as my weapons deal little to no damage against enemies without any mods equipped. Why force mod progression in a game mode that already has built-in stat progression? Why add evasion chance and crit rate to the mode? This isn’t an RPG, this is an action game. Victory and defeat should be determined by the player’s skill, not the roll of a dice. Overall, I’m extremely disappointed in this roguelike mode, which was the main draw for me.

There’s also something to be said about how every aspect of the game forces you to grind for mods, which, as far as I’m aware, are obtained through loot boxes. It’s the same song and dance we’ve seen so many times before. Exploit the gambling dopamine, get players addicted. Not surprising, just disappointing.

In the end, whether due to incompetence or a lack of time and resources, the game failed to meet my expectations despite all the big talk from the devs. If it’s the latter, I genuinely hope that, given enough time, they manage to turn this ship around. It might already be too late, but I hope they try their best. I’ll leave the game on my PC for a couple more days and see if I feel interested in booting it up again. If not, I’ll uninstall it and wait for further improvements.
